Count the bones.Middle ear: Three tiny bones (the smallest in the body) pass sound to the inner ear, and the smallest, the stapes, is about 3 mm long.
Count the bones.Giraffe's neck: Giraffes have the same count as nearly every mammal, humans included, but each neck bone is enormously stretched.
Count the bones.One human wrist: These small carpal bones sit in two rows and are why your wrist can bend and twist so flexibly.
Count the bones.Human face: These include the cheekbones and the upper jaw, with the lower jaw being the only one that moves.
Count the bones.Human skull: Only the lower jaw moves; the rest are knitted together by zigzag joints called sutures.
Count the bones.Rib cage: Twelve pairs of ribs protect the heart and lungs, though about 1 in 100 people has an extra cervical rib.
Count the bones.One human hand: Both hands together hold 54 bones, and hands and feet together contain more than half of the whole skeleton.
Count the bones.Baby's spine (vertebrae): As we grow, the lowest ones fuse into the sacrum and tailbone, so an adult has fewer separate spine bones.
Count the bones.Adult skeleton: The thigh bone is the longest and strongest of them all, and the adult count is lower than a baby's because bones fuse.
Count the bones.Newborn skeleton: Many are soft cartilage that fuses over time, and the skull's soft spots let the head squeeze through birth.

Old master paintings, by date.The Arnolfini Portrait: A mirror in this painting reflects two more figures, and Jan van Eyck wrote on the wall that he was there.
Old master paintings, by date.The Birth of Venus: Botticelli's Venus echoes ancient statues, and his Medici patrons commissioned the painting.
Old master paintings, by date.The Last Supper: Leonardo used experimental paint on dry plaster, which began to flake within decades, and the wall survived a 1943 bomb.
Old master paintings, by date.Mona Lisa: It was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, and the theft made it world famous.
Old master paintings, by date.The Creation of Adam: The near-touching fingers on the Sistine ceiling have become one of the most recognized images in art.
Old master paintings, by date.The Night Watch: It is not a night scene; dark varnish gave it the name, and the canvas was trimmed in 1715 to fit a wall.
Old master paintings, by date.Las Meninas: Velázquez put himself in the picture painting the royal family, and Picasso later painted 58 variations of it.
Old master paintings, by date.Girl with a Pearl Earring: It is a tronie, a character study, not a portrait, and Vermeer's use of an expensive blue pigment stands out.
Old master paintings, by date.The Great Wave off Kanagawa: It is technically a woodblock print, not a painting, and Mount Fuji is tiny in the background.
Old master paintings, by date.Washington Crossing Delaware: A German-based American painter made it, and the huge canvas has a flag that did not exist in 1776.

Distance from Honolulu.Kahului, Maui: Maui's main town and airport; the island's Haleakala volcano rises to about 3,055 metres.
Distance from Honolulu.Midway Atoll: The 1942 battle here turned the Pacific War; today it is a wildlife refuge with the world's largest colony of Laysan albatrosses.
Distance from Honolulu.San Francisco: Pan Am's China Clipper flying boats started their 1935 trans-Pacific service here, hopping via Honolulu and Midway to Manila.
Distance from Honolulu.Anchorage: Alaska's largest city sits near 61 degrees north, so summer days there stretch to nearly 19 hours of daylight.
Distance from Honolulu.Suva, Fiji: The capital of Fiji, on the island of Viti Levu, sits in one of the wettest parts of the country.
Distance from Honolulu.Tokyo: Japanese immigrants and their descendants form one of Hawaii's largest ethnic groups, so this city feels well connected to the islands.
Distance from Honolulu.Auckland: New Zealand's largest city is built on a volcanic field of roughly 50 volcanoes, with Rangitoto its youngest.
Distance from Honolulu.Sydney: Its Opera House's sail roof is covered with over a million tiles, designed by Jorn Utzon, who left before it opened.
Distance from Honolulu.London: Honolulu's clocks run 10 hours behind this city's in winter and 11 in summer, thanks to daylight saving time.
Distance from Honolulu.Cape Town: Table Mountain overlooks it, and it lies almost on the opposite side of the world from Hawaii.

Famous landmarks from north to south.Stonehenge: The stones are aligned with the summer solstice sunrise, and crowds still gather there each June to watch the Sun rise over them.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Eiffel Tower: It grows up to about 15 cm taller in summer, because the iron expands in the heat, and shrinks again in winter.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Leaning Tower of Pisa: It began leaning during construction because of soft ground; engineers stabilised it by 2001 and even straightened it slightly.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Colosseum: Its official name is the Flavian Amphitheatre; the nickname probably comes from a huge nearby statue, the Colossus of Nero.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Statue of Liberty: The copper skin is only about 2.4 mm thick, and its green colour comes from oxidation, since it was originally shiny brown.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Golden Gate Bridge: Its colour is 'International Orange', chosen to stand out against the fog and the landscape, and it is repainted continuously.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Great Pyramid of Giza: Its sides are aligned almost perfectly with the four compass directions, a feat of surveying nearly 4,500 years ago.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Taj Mahal: Built by Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, its four minarets lean slightly outward so they would fall away from the tomb.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Christ the Redeemer: The statue stands about 30 metres tall on Corcovado mountain, and it is struck by lightning several times a year.
Famous landmarks from north to south.Sydney Opera House: Designed by Danish architect Jorn Utzon, who left the project in a dispute over costs before it was completed in 1973.

Founded long ago, selling something else.Kongō Gumi (temple builders): The Japanese temple builders were founded in 578.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Beretta (gun barrels): Italy's Beretta started in Gardone Val Trompia making gun barrels for Venice's arsenal.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Peugeot (steel, pepper mills): The French family firm moved from steel to tools and pepper mills, then bicycles and cars.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Nokia (paper mill): The Finnish company went from paper to rubber boots, cables and then phones.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Nintendo (playing cards): Based in Kyoto, it made hanafuda playing cards.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Toyota (weaving looms): It was called Toyoda until it was renamed to something easier to say.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Lego (wooden toys): The name comes from the Danish 'leg godt', meaning 'play well'.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Samsung (groceries): It began in Daegu as a trading company exporting dried fish and groceries; the name means 'three stars'.
Founded long ago, selling something else.IKEA (pens and wallets): Ingvar Kamprad began it at 17; the name joins his initials with Elmtaryd and Agunnaryd, his farm and village.
Founded long ago, selling something else.Lamborghini (tractors): After a spat with Enzo Ferrari, Ferruccio Lamborghini turned from tractors to sports cars.

Molecules by molar mass.Hydrogen gas (H₂): Hydrogen gas is the lightest molecule, and each molecule holds two atoms of the most abundant element in the universe.
Molecules by molar mass.Helium: Helium is a single-atom gas, and it's so light that it escapes Earth's gravity, so we get it from underground reserves.
Molecules by molar mass.Methane: Methane is the main part of natural gas, and it traps far more heat than carbon dioxide over a short span.
Molecules by molar mass.Water: Water is just 18 g/mol, yet its hydrogen bonds make it unusually good at staying liquid, so life depends on it.
Molecules by molar mass.Nitrogen gas (N₂): Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air we breathe, and it's mostly inert, so it's used to fill snack bags.
Molecules by molar mass.Oxygen gas (O₂): Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of Earth's atmosphere, and it is essential for animals, which need it to release energy.
Molecules by molar mass.Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, and it is what puts the fizz in fizzy drinks and the rise in bread.
Molecules by molar mass.Table salt: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine ions, and it is the only rock humans commonly eat.
Molecules by molar mass.Glucose: Glucose is the sugar your body uses for energy, and your brain uses about a fifth of it.
Molecules by molar mass.Sucrose: Sucrose is ordinary table sugar, made by joining glucose and fructose, and it is extracted from sugar cane and beets.

Hit products through the ages.Coca-Cola: Invented by pharmacist John Pemberton in Atlanta, it was first sold at a soda fountain, reportedly at about nine glasses a day.
Hit products through the ages.Kodak Brownie camera: Selling for one dollar, it put photography within reach of ordinary people, including children, for the first time.
Hit products through the ages.Sliced bread: First sold in Missouri after Otto Rohwedder built a bread-slicing machine, giving us the phrase 'the best thing since sliced bread'.
Hit products through the ages.Slinky: A naval engineer knocked a tension spring off a shelf, watched it tumble, and realized it could be a toy.
Hit products through the ages.Barbie: Named after co-founder Ruth Handler's daughter Barbara, she debuted at the New York Toy Fair in March 1959.
Hit products through the ages.Pong: Atari's engineer Al Alcorn built it as a warm-up exercise, but the game was so addictive that the company shipped it.
Hit products through the ages.Windows 1.0: It ran on top of MS-DOS and used tiled rather than overlapping windows, years before Windows became a household name.
Hit products through the ages.Furby: Sold over forty million in its first three years, it was reportedly banned from the NSA's premises over fears it might repeat secrets.
Hit products through the ages.iPhone: Steve Jobs unveiled it in January 2007 as three products in one: a phone, an iPod and an internet communicator.
Hit products through the ages.Pokémon Go: It was downloaded over 500 million times within months, sending players outdoors to hunt creatures on real streets.

When these nations won independence.United States: The US declared independence from Britain in 1776, and the Declaration was signed in Philadelphia, and it was largely written by Thomas Jefferson.
When these nations won independence.Haiti: Haiti became the first country to be founded by a successful slave revolt, and the first independent Black republic.
When these nations won independence.Brazil: Brazil's independence came when Prince Pedro, the Portuguese king's son, declared 'Independence or death' and became its emperor.
When these nations won independence.Belgium: Belgium broke from the Netherlands after a revolt that reportedly began after an opera performance in Brussels.
When these nations won independence.Finland: Finland gained independence after the Russian Revolution, and it endured a short civil war soon after.
When these nations won independence.India: India won independence from Britain, but the partition created Pakistan, causing one of the largest migrations in history.
When these nations won independence.Ghana: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
When these nations won independence.Algeria: Algeria gained independence from France after a brutal war of about eight years.
When these nations won independence.Bangladesh: Bangladesh broke away from Pakistan after a war, and was helped by India's intervention.
When these nations won independence.Croatia: Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia, and a war followed that lasted until 1995.

How far you travel in these events.The mile: Roger Bannister first broke four minutes for it in 1954, and the distance comes from the Roman mille passus, a thousand paces.
How far you travel in these events.Steeplechase: The 3,000 m race has 28 barriers and 7 water jumps, and its name comes from horse races that aimed for a church steeple.
How far you travel in these events.Ironman swim: The Ironman began in Hawaii in 1978 as a bet over which sport produced the fittest athletes, swimmers, cyclists or runners.
How far you travel in these events.Olympic triathlon run: Triathletes run this after swimming 1.5 km and cycling 40 km, so the legs feel like jelly by the time they start.
How far you travel in these events.Half marathon: The Great North Run in Newcastle is among the world's largest half marathons, with tens of thousands of finishers each year.
How far you travel in these events.English Channel swim: Captain Matthew Webb first swam it unaided in 1875, taking almost 22 hours, and currents mean most swimmers cover far more than the straight line.
How far you travel in these events.Marathon: The odd 42.195 km comes from the 1908 London Olympics, where the course ran from Windsor Castle to the stadium.
How far you travel in these events.Olympic long race walk: Walkers must always keep one foot on the ground, and judges can disqualify them for lifting; the 50 km race was dropped after Tokyo 2020.
How far you travel in these events.Ironman bike leg: Drafting is banned in an Ironman, so riders must stay several bike lengths apart, unlike in road racing where packs shelter each other.
How far you travel in these events.Tour de France (whole): The first Tour in 1903 had just six stages, and the modern race runs 21 stages over about 23 days.

TV family sitcoms by premiere year.I Love Lucy: It pioneered filming on 35mm in front of a live audience with three cameras, and Lucille Ball's pregnancy was written into the show.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.The Flintstones: It was the first animated series in prime time.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.The Brady Bunch: Its opening shows the family in a grid of nine squares.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.Happy Days: It spun off Mork and Mindy and Laverne and Shirley.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.The Cosby Show: It revived the sitcom genre and stayed number one for five seasons.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.The Simpsons: Born as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show, it became America's longest-running animated series.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air: Will Smith famously got the role after meeting Quincy Jones at a party.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.Everybody Loves Raymond: It was based on Ray Romano's stand-up routines about his family.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.Malcolm in the Middle: It broke the mold by dropping the laugh track and using single-camera filming.
TV family sitcoms by premiere year.Modern Family: A mockumentary-style show that won five straight Emmys for best comedy series, from 2010 to 2014.

When these role-playing games came out.Ultima: Richard Garriott made it in his bedroom, using the in-game name 'Lord British'.
When these role-playing games came out.Dragon Quest: Dragon Quest's look was drawn by Akira Toriyama of Dragon Ball, and it's nearly a national obsession in Japan.
When these role-playing games came out.The Elder Scrolls: Arena: The first Elder Scrolls game began as a gladiator-arena game before becoming an open world.
When these role-playing games came out.Chrono Trigger: A dream team of Final Fantasy's Sakaguchi, Dragon Quest's Horii and Toriyama made it.
When these role-playing games came out.Baldur's Gate: BioWare's game used Dungeons & Dragons rules and helped bring RPGs to the PC; a third instalment arrived in 2023.
When these role-playing games came out.Fable: Peter Molyneux's game had your choices change your hero's looks, so good deeds brought a halo and evil brought horns.
When these role-playing games came out.Mass Effect: BioWare's sci-fi trilogy carries your choices across games through saved files.
When these role-playing games came out.Skyrim: Shouts of the Dragonborn and the 'arrow in the knee' meme made it a pop culture staple.
When these role-playing games came out.The Witcher 3: Based on Andrzej Sapkowski's books, CD Projekt Red's game sold over 50 million copies.
When these role-playing games came out.Elden Ring: FromSoftware worked with George R. R. Martin on its backstory, and it sold over 20 million quickly.

When these financial institutions were f.Monte dei Paschi di Siena: Often called the world's oldest surviving bank, it is based in Siena, Italy.
When these financial institutions were f.Amsterdam Stock Exchange: Founded by the Dutch East India Company, it traded the first publicly sold shares.
When these financial institutions were f.Bank of England: It was created to raise funds for a war against France, and is nicknamed the 'Old Lady of Threadneedle Street'.
When these financial institutions were f.New York Stock Exchange: It began as the Buttonwood Agreement, signed by brokers meeting under a tree on Wall Street.
When these financial institutions were f.HSBC: Founded to finance trade between Hong Kong and Shanghai, its name is short for the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation.
When these financial institutions were f.Goldman Sachs: Founded by Marcus Goldman in New York, who started by trading commercial paper.
When these financial institutions were f.US Federal Reserve: Created after repeated financial panics, notably 1907, it was signed into law by Woodrow Wilson.
When these financial institutions were f.IMF: Created at the Bretton Woods conference, it was meant to stabilize currencies after the war.
When these financial institutions were f.Nasdaq: It was the world's first electronic stock market, with quotes on screens rather than a trading floor.
When these financial institutions were f.European Central Bank: Based in Frankfurt, it controls the euro's monetary policy for a currency used by about 20 countries.

Landmarks of the printed word, by year.The Gutenberg Bible: About 180 copies were printed, and roughly 49 survive in whole or in part.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.King James Bible: Its rhythms gave English phrases like 'the powers that be' and 'a labour of love'.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Shakespeare's First Folio: It collected 36 plays, 18 of which might otherwise have been lost, including Macbeth.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Johnson's Dictionary: Samuel Johnson wrote it largely alone in about nine years, famously defining 'oats' as food for horses in England.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Encyclopaedia Britannica: It was first published in Edinburgh in installments and grew into a famous multi-volume reference.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Webster's Dictionary: Noah Webster pushed American spellings like 'color' and 'center'.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Roget's Thesaurus: Peter Mark Roget, a physician, compiled it and gave English a way to find a word from an idea.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Oxford English Dictionary: Work began in the 1850s, and the first edition took about 70 years to finish.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Guinness Book of Records: The Guinness brewery commissioned it to settle pub arguments, starting with the fastest game bird.
Landmarks of the printed word, by year.Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched it in January 2001.

How scratch-resistant these are.Baby powder (talc): The softest mineral on the scale, it is the main ingredient of baby powder, and even a fingernail can scratch it.
How scratch-resistant these are.Fingernail: At 2.5 it scratches gypsum but not calcite, a quick field test geologists use.
How scratch-resistant these are.Copper coin: Calcite is a 3 and so is a copper coin, so each can barely scratch the other.
How scratch-resistant these are.Iron nail: Geologists carry a steel nail or knife as a hardness tool to test minerals like fluorite and apatite.
How scratch-resistant these are.Window glass: Glass is the benchmark that minerals must scratch, and a steel knife blade sits about the same.
How scratch-resistant these are.Steel file: Quartz can scratch this file, while feldspar sits near it on the scale.
How scratch-resistant these are.Quartz: One of Earth's most common minerals and the main ingredient of sand, which is why sand can scratch glass.
How scratch-resistant these are.Topaz: A gem that comes in many colors; the pink-orange kind is called imperial topaz.
How scratch-resistant these are.Sapphire watch crystal: Sapphire is corundum, the same mineral as ruby, and its toughness makes watch crystals nearly scratch-proof.
How scratch-resistant these are.Diamond: The hardest natural material, though brittle; in absolute terms it is several times harder than the mineral at 9.

US state capitals from north to south.Juneau: No road links it to the rest of Alaska, so it is reached only by sea or air. It's named for a gold prospector, Joe Juneau.
US state capitals from north to south.Olympia: Sits at the southern end of Puget Sound and takes its name from the nearby Olympic Mountains. The capital is far smaller than Seattle.
US state capitals from north to south.Boise: The name comes from the French for "wooded", and French-Canadian trappers are said to have praised the trees along the river as they approached.
US state capitals from north to south.Albany: Dutch traders built Fort Orange here in the 1620s, making it one of the oldest European settlements in the original 13 states.
US state capitals from north to south.Denver: Known as the Mile High City because of its elevation of 5,280 feet. The thin air makes baseballs fly farther at Coors Field.
US state capitals from north to south.Sacramento: The state's capital grew during the Gold Rush of the 1840s and 1850s, near the point where the American and Sacramento rivers meet.
US state capitals from north to south.Nashville: Known as Music City, home to the Grand Ole Opry, and it has a full-size replica of the Parthenon in Centennial Park.
US state capitals from north to south.Phoenix: Named after the mythical bird that rises from ashes, since the city was built atop the remains of ancient Hohokam irrigation canals.
US state capitals from north to south.Austin: The "live music capital of the world" is also home to a colony of over a million bats living under the Congress Avenue Bridge.
US state capitals from north to south.Honolulu: The only US state capital in the tropics. Its Iolani Palace was the official residence of Hawaiian monarchs, and it had electric lights before the White House.

How old these great minds were when they.Évariste Galois: The French mathematician died after a duel at 20, and he wrote down his ideas on the night before.
How old these great minds were when they.Srinivasa Ramanujan: Ramanujan was a self-taught Indian mathematician who sent his results to Hardy, and he died at 32.
How old these great minds were when they.Heinrich Hertz: Hertz proved that electromagnetic waves exist, and the unit of frequency is named for him.
How old these great minds were when they.Blaise Pascal: Pascal contributed to probability and the physics of pressure, and the unit of pressure is named for him.
How old these great minds were when they.Antoine Lavoisier: Lavoisier was a father of modern chemistry who was guillotined in the French Revolution.
How old these great minds were when they.Marie Curie: Marie Curie won two Nobel Prizes in different sciences, and her notebooks are still radioactive.
How old these great minds were when they.Charles Darwin: Darwin spent five years aboard the Beagle, and he published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
How old these great minds were when they.Galileo Galilei: Galileo spent his last years under house arrest, and he improved the telescope.
How old these great minds were when they.Isaac Newton: Newton wrote the Principia and invented calculus, and he was also Master of the Royal Mint.
How old these great minds were when they.Nikola Tesla: Tesla had many patents, and he died in a New York hotel room in 1943 with little money.

Fractions by value.1/3: As a decimal it never ends, which is why splitting a bill three ways always leaves a stray cent.
Fractions by value.3/8: Common in inches, it's a standard drill bit and socket size, and equals exactly 0.375.
Fractions by value.2/5: It ends neatly as 0.4, because denominators made only of 2s and 5s always give tidy decimals.
Fractions by value.4/9: Any ninths repeat their numerator forever: 4/9 is 0.444…, and 5/9 is 0.555…, a handy shortcut.
Fractions by value.1/2: In music a half note lasts half of a whole note, and British players call it a minim.
Fractions by value.5/9: It's the key to temperature conversion: subtract 32 from Fahrenheit, then multiply by 5/9 to get Celsius.
Fractions by value.3/5: The 1787 US 'three-fifths compromise' counted each enslaved person as this fraction of a person when allotting seats in Congress.
Fractions by value.2/3: Ancient Egyptian scribes wrote most fractions as sums of unit fractions, but gave 2/3 its own special symbol.
Fractions by value.5/7: Sevenths repeat in a six-digit cycle. 1/7 is 0.142857…, and 5/7 is the same digits rotated, 0.714285….
Fractions by value.7/8: It is exactly 0.111 in binary, which is why eighths turn up so often in computing and old stock prices.

When these dinosaurs got their names.Megalosaurus: Its name means 'great lizard' and it was the first dinosaur ever scientifically described, by William Buckland in 1824.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Archaeopteryx: Its name means 'ancient wing', and the fossils of this feathered creature found in Bavaria were quickly used as evidence for evolution after Darwin's book.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Stegosaurus: Its name means 'roof lizard', and the plates on its back probably worked as temperature regulators or for display, not armour.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Triceratops: Its name means 'three-horned face', and its skull could be a third of the animal's body length, with a frill that probably served to display.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Tyrannosaurus rex: Henry Fairfield Osborn gave it a name meaning 'tyrant lizard king', and its bite was strong enough to crush bone, as shown by bite marks.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Spinosaurus: It was named by the German palaeontologist Ernst Stromer, and the original fossils were destroyed in a World War II bombing raid.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Velociraptor: Its name means 'swift robber', and it was in fact about turkey-sized and feathered, quite different from the film depiction.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Deinonychus: Its name means 'terrible claw', and its discovery in 1964 led scientists to rethink whether dinosaurs were warm-blooded.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Argentinosaurus: Named for Argentina, it is one of the largest land animals known, perhaps 70 tons, and it was found in Patagonia from fragments of vertebrae.
When these dinosaurs got their names.Microraptor: Its fossils from China show four wings, with long feathers on both its arms and legs, making it one of the smallest known dinosaurs.

The 1860s, one event per year.Lincoln elected: He won the presidency without carrying a single southern state, and seven of them seceded before he took office.
The 1860s, one event per year.Kingdom of Italy proclaimed: Victor Emmanuel II became its first king, and Turin served as the first capital until Rome joined in 1871.
The 1860s, one event per year.Bismarck becomes Prussian PM: Soon afterwards he said Germany would be united by 'iron and blood', not by speeches, and went on to build the German Empire.
The 1860s, one event per year.Battle of Gettysburg: Over three days in July 1863 it produced about 50,000 casualties, the bloodiest battle of the Civil War.
The 1860s, one event per year.First Geneva Convention: Henri Dunant, shocked by the carnage of Solferino, inspired it. It led to the Red Cross and rules to protect the wounded.
The 1860s, one event per year.Lincoln assassinated: John Wilkes Booth shot him at Ford's Theatre just days after Lee surrendered.
The 1860s, one event per year.Austro-Prussian War: Prussia crushed Austria in about seven weeks, and the conflict is known as the Seven Weeks' War.
The 1860s, one event per year.US buys Alaska: The 7.2 million dollar price was around two cents an acre, and critics mocked it as 'Seward's Folly'.
The 1860s, one event per year.Meiji Restoration: It ended 250 years of shogun rule, returned power to the emperor, and Edo was soon renamed Tokyo.
The 1860s, one event per year.Suez Canal opens: Ferdinand de Lesseps's canal let ships skip the long route around Africa, cutting thousands of kilometres from journeys to Asia.

Web browsers by first release.WorldWideWeb: Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first web browser on a NeXT computer, and it doubled as an editor. It was later renamed Nexus.
Web browsers by first release.Lynx: This text-only browser from the University of Kansas is still maintained, and it shows how pages appear to screen readers.
Web browsers by first release.Mosaic: Developed at the University of Illinois, its inline images helped make the web mainstream, and Marc Andreessen worked on it.
Web browsers by first release.Netscape Navigator: It dominated the mid-1990s and introduced JavaScript, written by Brendan Eich in about ten days.
Web browsers by first release.Internet Explorer: Bundling it with Windows triggered antitrust battles, and Microsoft finally retired it in 2022.
Web browsers by first release.Safari: Apple's browser uses WebKit, an engine that also gave Google Chrome its early start.
Web browsers by first release.Firefox: Born from Netscape's code, it ended Internet Explorer's dominance, and its mascot is a fiery red panda.
Web browsers by first release.Google Chrome: It launched alongside a comic book explaining its design, and its V8 engine made JavaScript much faster.
Web browsers by first release.Microsoft Edge: It replaced Internet Explorer, then was rebuilt in 2020 on Chromium, the same engine Chrome uses.
Web browsers by first release.Vivaldi: Opera co-founder Jon von Tetzchner started this browser, named after the composer, with deep customization.

Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Challenger Deep: The deepest known point in the ocean, in the Mariana Trench, has pressure over a thousand times that at the surface.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.The Titanic's wreck: The wreck lies about 3,800 m down in two main pieces, with the bow and stern hundreds of meters apart.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Dead Sea shore: This is the lowest land on Earth's surface, and the water is so salty that swimmers float effortlessly.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Denver: The Mile High City marks the exact altitude with a step on the Colorado Capitol.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Mexico City: Built on an ancient lake bed, the city is slowly sinking in places.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.La Paz, Bolivia: This Bolivian capital is the highest seat of national government in the world, with a cable car commuter network.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Kilimanjaro summit: Africa's tallest peak is a volcano, and its glaciers are shrinking fast.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.Everest summit: It grows by roughly 4 mm a year as tectonic plates collide.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.A cruising airliner: At that height the outside air is around -55 °C, and passengers rely on pressurized cabins.
Altitude, from ocean floor to orbit.The ISS: It circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so astronauts see about 16 sunrises a day.

Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Novarupta (Katmai), Alaska: The largest eruption of the 20th century, it created the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, and nearby Katmai was blamed at first.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Lassen Peak, California: Lassen Peak erupted from 1914 to 1917, the only Cascade volcano besides St Helens to erupt in the contiguous US last century.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Paricutín, Mexico: It was born in a Mexican cornfield in 1943, watched by farmer Dionisio Pulido, and rose 336 m in its first year.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Mount St. Helens: The May 18 eruption started with a huge landslide, killed 57 people, and removed about 400 m from the summit.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.El Chichón, Mexico: This little-known volcano in Chiapas killed about 2,000 people, and its sulfur cloud cooled global climate slightly.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia: A mudflow, or lahar, buried the town of Armero and killed about 23,000 people, one of the deadliest volcanic disasters.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Redoubt, Alaska: A KLM jumbo jet flew into its ash cloud in 1989 and lost all four engines, but landed safely in Anchorage.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Soufrière Hills, Montserrat: It destroyed Plymouth, Montserrat's capital, and drove roughly two-thirds of residents off the island.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Chaitén, Chile: It erupted with no warning after thousands of years of quiet, forcing a whole town to evacuate.
Eruptions in the Americas, in order.Fuego, Guatemala: A deadly pyroclastic flow in June 2018 killed over 100 people and buried villages near the volcano.

The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Laius warned by an oracle: An oracle warned King Laius that his son would kill him, setting the whole self-fulfilling tragedy in motion.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Baby left on a mountain: His ankles were pierced and bound, hence the name Oedipus, which means 'swollen foot'.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Raised in Corinth: King Polybus and Queen Merope adopted him, and he grew up believing they were his real parents.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Consults Delphi: The oracle told him he would kill his father and marry his mother. To escape that, he fled Corinth, straight toward Thebes.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Kills a man at a crossroads: At a three-way crossroads he fought an old man and killed him, not knowing he was his father, Laius.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Solves the Sphinx's riddle: The riddle asked what walks on four legs, then two, then three. The answer is man.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Marries Jocasta: Thebes rewarded its savior with the throne and the widowed queen, who was in fact his own mother.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Plague strikes Thebes: In Sophocles' play, a plague opens the story. The oracle says it will end when Laius's killer is found.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.The truth comes out: The blind prophet Tiresias hints at the truth first, but Oedipus refuses to believe it. Sophocles' play is a model of dramatic irony.
The tragedy of Oedipus, in story order.Blinds himself: After Jocasta takes her own life, he puts out his eyes with her brooches. Freud later named a complex after him.

Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Bunsen burner: The Bunsen burner, named for Robert Bunsen, mixes gas and air for a hot, clean blue flame, and was developed with Peter Desaga.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Erlenmeyer flask: Emil Erlenmeyer's conical flask is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so you can swirl liquids without spilling.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Autoclave: Charles Chamberland invented the autoclave, a pressure cooker that sterilizes equipment, and it's still used in hospitals.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Petri dish: Julius Petri was an assistant to Robert Koch, and his flat dish helped grow bacteria and showed that diseases have specific germs.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Cloud chamber: C. T. R. Wilson invented the cloud chamber after watching clouds on Ben Nevis, and it first revealed trails of subatomic particles.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Mass spectrograph: Francis Aston built this device to separate atoms by mass, and it showed that many elements have isotopes.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Electron microscope: Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope, and won the Nobel Prize in 1986, 55 years later.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Gel electrophoresis: Gel electrophoresis separates molecules by size using an electric field, and it's how DNA fingerprinting works.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.Scanning tunneling microscope: Binnig and Rohrer's microscope can image single atoms by scanning a tiny tip over a surface, and won a Nobel Prize in 1986.
Lab equipment, by when it was introduced.PCR (DNA copying): Kary Mullis invented PCR and won a Nobel Prize; the process is why a tiny DNA sample can be copied millions of times, and it's central to COVID tests.

Career totals of retired greats.Michael Jordan's NBA titles: He lost no NBA Finals series in six tries, and was named MVP in all six.
Career totals of retired greats.Arnold Palmer's majors: 'Arnie's Army' of fans helped bring golf to television, and he won seven majors.
Career totals of retired greats.Ben Hogan's majors: He came back to win after a 1949 car crash that nearly killed him.
Career totals of retired greats.Bjorn Borg's Slams: He retired at 26 with 11 Slams, including five straight Wimbledon titles.
Career totals of retired greats.Pete Sampras's Slams: Seven of them were at Wimbledon, in a career built around one of the best serves in tennis history.
Career totals of retired greats.Jack Nicklaus's majors: The 'Golden Bear' also finished second in a record 19 majors.
Career totals of retired greats.Roger Federer's Slams: He won eight Wimbledon titles, more than any other man.
Career totals of retired greats.Rafael Nadal's Slams: Fourteen of his titles came at the French Open, a record for any player at a single Slam.
Career totals of retired greats.Michael Phelps's golds: His career total of 28 medals made him the most decorated Olympian ever.
Career totals of retired greats.Margaret Court's Slams: She also won the calendar-year Grand Slam in 1970, and holds the all-time record for singles majors.

Cities by elevation.Jericho: It's among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with roots going back roughly 10,000 years.
Cities by elevation.Venice: It's built on islands in a lagoon, and a flood barrier called MOSE protects it from high tides.
Cities by elevation.Las Vegas: Its Spanish name means 'the meadows', after springs that once watered the desert valley.
Cities by elevation.Jerusalem: The ancient city sits in the Judean hills, so pilgrims are said to 'go up' to it.
Cities by elevation.Salt Lake City: It hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics, and lies beside the Great Salt Lake.
Cities by elevation.Denver: Called the Mile High City, its altitude means a baseball hit there travels farther.
Cities by elevation.Johannesburg: Founded in 1886 after a gold rush, it sits on the high plateau, the Highveld.
Cities by elevation.Aspen: It began as a silver-mining boom town, then became a famed ski resort.
Cities by elevation.Cusco: It was the capital of the Inca empire, and visitors often drink coca tea to combat altitude sickness.
Cities by elevation.Lhasa: Home to the Potala Palace, it's among the highest large cities in the world.

Units of pressure.Pascal: Named for the French scientist Blaise Pascal. One pascal is tiny: a banknote lying flat presses down with about a pascal.
Units of pressure.Millibar: Forecasters long used it: sea-level air pressure is about 1,013 millibars, and a strong hurricane drops well below 950.
Units of pressure.Millimetre of mercury: Born of the mercury barometer and still used for blood pressure. A healthy reading of 120 over 80 is in these units.
Units of pressure.Inch of water: Handy for tiny pressures like gas lines and ventilation ducts. It equals the pressure at the bottom of a one-inch column of water.
Units of pressure.Kilopascal: Tyre gauges in much of the world use it. A typical car tyre sits around 220 kPa.
Units of pressure.Inch of mercury: US weather reports and pilots' altimeter settings quote it. Standard sea-level pressure is about 29.92 inches of mercury.
Units of pressure.Pound per square inch: The US favourite for tyres and compressors. Ordinary air at sea level presses on you at roughly 14.7 psi.
Units of pressure.Bar: About one atmosphere. Scuba divers gain roughly one bar of pressure for every 10 metres of seawater they descend.
Units of pressure.Megapascal: A million pascals, the scale of hydraulics and tough materials. Steel's strength is often quoted in hundreds of megapascals.
Units of pressure.Kip per square inch: A 'kip' is a kilopound, 1,000 pounds-force, so American engineers use ksi to describe the strength of steel and concrete.

How long the elite take to finish.50 m freestyle: The shortest Olympic swimming race is often decided by hundredths of a second, which is why touchpads matter.
How long the elite take to finish.400 m run: One full lap. Wayde van Niekerk's 43.03 world record from Rio 2016 came from the outside lane, 8.
How long the elite take to finish.100 m breaststroke: Adam Peaty was the first to break 58 seconds in the 100 m breaststroke, and went on to dominate it.
How long the elite take to finish.200 m freestyle: World records set during the 2009 'supersuit' era, in polyurethane suits, were so fast that the suits were later banned.
How long the elite take to finish.1500 m run: The 'metric mile'. Hicham El Guerrouj's 3:26 from 1998 still stands as the world record.
How long the elite take to finish.1500 m freestyle: Long a men's Olympic event, the women's version joined in 2020, where Katie Ledecky dominates.
How long the elite take to finish.10,000 m run: Twenty-five laps of the track. Joshua Cheptegei's world record is about 26 minutes 11 seconds.
How long the elite take to finish.Half marathon: The 13.1 miles are roughly half the classic distance. Elite men have gone under 57 minutes.
How long the elite take to finish.Marathon: Kelvin Kiptum ran 2:00:35 in 2023. Eliud Kipchoge's unofficial sub-two-hour run in 2019 used rotating pacers.
How long the elite take to finish.Ironman triathlon (pro): The event is swim 3.8 km, ride 180 km, run 42.2 km. It grew out of a 1977 barroom debate in Hawaii about who is fittest.

Vitamin C per 100 grams.Apple: Apples are low in vitamin C, but their peel holds much of their fibre and polyphenols.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Banana: Bananas are better known for potassium, which makes them very slightly radioactive. It is harmless.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Strawberry: About 150 grams of strawberries gives roughly a full day's vitamin C. Botanically, the seeds on the outside make them no true berry.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Kiwi: Originally called the Chinese gooseberry, it was renamed kiwifruit for export in the 1950s.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Red bell pepper: A red bell pepper is a fully ripened green one, with more vitamin C and beta-carotene.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Blackcurrant: Britain's wartime blackcurrant syrup, Ribena, was promoted to give children vitamin C when oranges were unavailable.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Guava: Guava has more than four times the vitamin C of an orange.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Rose hip: British children collected rose hips in World War II for vitamin C syrup when citrus was scarce.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Acerola cherry: A small Caribbean cherry with roughly 30 times the vitamin C of an orange.
Vitamin C per 100 grams.Kakadu plum: An Australian Aboriginal bush food and one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C known.

Comic book movies by release.Superman (Reeve): Christopher Reeve's Man of Steel was sold with the tagline "You'll believe a man can fly." John Williams's theme is instantly recognisable.
Comic book movies by release.Batman (Keaton): Tim Burton's film made Batman a dark blockbuster and launched a wave of merchandise. Danny Elfman wrote its famous score.
Comic book movies by release.The Crow: Based on James O'Barr's comic, it became a cult classic after lead actor Brandon Lee died during filming. Its gothic look was widely copied.
Comic book movies by release.Blade: Wesley Snipes starred in this Marvel vampire hunter film. Many credit it with proving comic films could succeed before the superhero boom.
Comic book movies by release.X-Men: Bryan Singer's film started the modern superhero era at Fox. It ran with Hugh Jackman's Wolverine for decades.
Comic book movies by release.Spider-Man (Raimi): Sam Raimi's film was the first to take over $100 million in a single weekend in the US. Tobey Maguire wore the suit.
Comic book movies by release.Hellboy: Guillermo del Toro's film is based on Mike Mignola's comic. Ron Perlman played the demon who files down his own horns.
Comic book movies by release.Watchmen: Alan Moore's graphic novel was long called unfilmable. Zack Snyder's movie kept the Cold War setting and the doomsday clock.
Comic book movies by release.Wonder Woman: This film was the first big-budget superhero film directed by a woman, Patty Jenkins. It was set in the First World War.
Comic book movies by release.Joker: Joaquin Phoenix won the Best Actor Oscar for this origin story. It was the first R-rated comic book film to take a billion dollars.

How long until it's ready?.Espresso shot: Pressurised water is forced through finely ground coffee in about half a minute. The foamy layer on top is called crema.
How long until it's ready?.Wood-fired pizza: A true Neapolitan oven runs at about 450 degrees Celsius, so the pizza cooks in roughly a minute and a half. Naples's traditional pizza has UNESCO recognition.
How long until it's ready?.Instant noodles: Momofuku Ando invented them in Japan in 1958. Pre-fried and dried noodles rehydrate quickly in hot water, and they became a global staple.
How long until it's ready?.Hard-boiled egg: Older eggs are easier to peel than very fresh ones, because the membrane clings less once the egg's pH rises with age.
How long until it's ready?.Bread dough's first rise: Yeast eats sugars in the dough and releases carbon dioxide, which makes bubbles. The dough usually doubles in size during this proving.
How long until it's ready?.Jelly setting in the fridge: Gelatin comes from animal collagen, and it sets as it cools. Fresh pineapple, kiwi and papaya contain enzymes that stop it from setting.
How long until it's ready?.Cold brew coffee: Steeping grounds in cold water for hours gives a smoother, less acidic coffee. It takes much longer than hot brewing because cold water extracts slowly.
How long until it's ready?.Sourdough starter from scratch: Flour and water gather wild yeast and lactic bacteria into a living culture. Some bakeries keep starters that are many decades old.
How long until it's ready?.Sauerkraut: Shredded cabbage ferments in its own salty juices, with lactic acid bacteria making it sour. Sailors ate it to avoid scurvy because it keeps vitamin C.
How long until it's ready?.Homemade vanilla extract: Vanilla pods soak in alcohol, usually vodka, for months. Vanilla is the second most expensive spice after saffron, as the orchid must be pollinated by hand.

Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.J.R.R. Tolkien born: He was born in Bloemfontein, South Africa, and moved to England aged three.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.The Hobbit: It was published by Allen and Unwin after the publisher's ten-year-old son reviewed the manuscript favourably.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.The Fellowship of the Ring: The Lord of the Rings was published in three volumes since a single book would have been costly.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.The Return of the King: It includes extensive appendices on languages, Elvish script and timelines.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.Tolkien dies: He died in Bournemouth and is buried in Oxford beside his wife, with the names Luthien and Beren on the gravestone.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.The Silmarillion: His son Christopher edited the book for publication after his death.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.Bakshi's animated LOTR: Ralph Bakshi's film used rotoscoping, drawing over live-action footage, and told only half the story.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.Jackson's Fellowship film: Peter Jackson filmed all three films at once in New Zealand over 438 days.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.Jackson's Return of the King: It won all 11 Oscars it was nominated for, tying Ben-Hur and Titanic.
Tolkien's life and Middle-earth.An Unexpected Journey: It began Jackson's Hobbit trilogy, shot at 48 frames per second, an unusual rate.

Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Gimel: The third letter's name is thought to come from gamal, meaning camel, and its shape is often said to show a camel's neck and head.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.He: The fifth letter doubles as the definite article, the, when attached to a word's front, and it is also one of two letters repeated in God's name in the Tetragrammaton.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Zayin: The seventh letter's name also means weapon in modern Hebrew, and its shape looks a little like a sword or a spear.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Yod: The smallest letter, its name means hand; it is the tenth letter, and also the first letter of the Tetragrammaton, God's name.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Kaf: Its name means palm, as in the palm of the hand, and it is one of five letters written differently at the end of a word.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Lamed: It is the tallest letter in the alphabet, rising above the line, and its shape is often compared to an ox goad, which the name may mean.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Nun: Its name means fish in Aramaic, it has a distinct final form, and Nun is also the name of Joshua's father in the Bible.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Ayin: Its name means eye, and its shape is a pair of eyes in the ancient Phoenician script, which this letter descends from.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Qof: Its name may mean the back of the head, and in modern Hebrew a similar word, kof, also means monkey.
Hebrew letters, by numeric value.Shin: It is written on tefillin and mezuzah cases as an abbreviation for Shaddai, a name of God, and its numeric value is 300.
